claims.text: The feedstock is gas-atomized AlCrFeNiSi powder with a particle-size distribution suitable for LPBF.
The AlCrFeNiSi powder exhibits intrinsic microstructural heterogeneities.
Beam oscillation at approximately 300–500 Hz and ±50–100 µm amplitude can be integrated into an LPBF scanning strategy for this feedstock.
The proposed LPBF processing window is approximately 240–260 W laser power and 700–850 mm/s scan speed.
The proposed components can be fabricated in an inert argon atmosphere.
The proposed processing window is applicable to miniature LPBF component geometries.
Beam oscillation produces a more spatially uniform heat distribution and melt pool.
Beam oscillation produces a refined, equiaxed microstructure.
Beam oscillation disperses instantaneous laser heat input over a wider area by spatially and temporally modulating the energy.
Dispersing the heat input reduces localized thermal-gradient intensity.
Reduced localized thermal gradients minimize residual-stress accumulation during rapid solidification.
Beam oscillation promotes homogeneous nucleation and consequent microstructural refinement.
Oscillated LPBF components will have lower residual thermal stresses than non-oscillated LPBF components.
Oscillated LPBF components will exhibit less distortion and warping than non-oscillated components.
Oscillated LPBF components will exhibit increased ductility and yield strength relative to non-oscillated components.
A conventional non-oscillatory, bidirectional line-scanning LPBF protocol is a feasible baseline process.
Scaling the strategy to larger builds or other material systems may require recalibration of oscillation parameters.
A greater-than-10% statistically significant reduction in residual stress is proposed as an improvement criterion.

contradictions.description: The headline hypothesis uses conventional high-energy deposition methods as the comparator, whereas the baseline and predicted outcome use otherwise similar non-oscillatory LPBF. These are not necessarily the same comparator.

The conditions specify post-build characterization under ambient conditions, while the falsification experiment calls for in-situ X-ray diffraction mapping, leaving the timing and environment of residual-stress measurement inconsistent or unclear.
